author: Don Reid
title: Coldwater gathers to honor late public safety chief - NewsBreak
text:
By Don Reid ,
1 days ago COLDWATER, MI. — The funeral of the city's Director of Public Safety, Joseph Scheid, 54, filled the Dearth Center at the Fairgrounds Tuesday, Aug. 11.
Dozens of law enforcement officers from agencies across Michigan attended to honor Scheid, along with his family, friends, and the local community. Scheid died suddenly Aug. 3 at work.
Two of the three directors under whom Scheid served, Gary Chester, who hired him, and Mark Bartell, whom he replaced, acted as pallbearers.
After the service, a procession with police, fire, and city vehicles joined law enforcement and the public in a procession that tied up traffic for over half an hour in downtown Coldwater to Oak Grove Cemetery on U.S. 12 by the Coldwater River, where he was buried.
Scheid joined the Coldwater department in December 1996 and rose to Deputy Director of Public Safety in 2016 and to Director of Public Safety in 2019.
The procession went by the Public Safety Building on Division Street.
During the funeral, family, friends, and fellow officers remembered Scheid as a big-hearted public servant whose life revolved around family, community, and service.
More: Coldwater mourns loss of public safety director
Speakers described him as a man of dignity, moral obligation, and quiet strength, someone who consistently chose to serve others in his work and personal life.
Pastor Mark Case framed his life in Christian faith, emphasizing that Scheid "lived his life to serve others" and that his legacy endures in the lives he shaped and the memories he left.
From the law enforcement side, Deputy Police Chief Pat Beeman and Bartell painted a picture of a deeply connected, approachable leader who knew people across schools, businesses, churches, and police departments.
They recalled his long work in drug enforcement, treatment, and prevention, his years as a K-9 officer, and his commitment to protecting his officers while trying to leave the department "a little better" than he found it.
Both men stressed his compassion for people down on their luck and his loyalty to his colleagues. Beeman urged officers to honor him by continuing to perform, "One breath at a time, one step at a time, one day at a time," even while grieving.
Both his daughters added the personal dimension: Scheid as the unconventional but devoted "girl dad" who built toughness and confidence through sports, outdoor adventures, and constant support.
His older sister, Lisa Wallbaum, told stories about a younger Scheid and their upbringing in rural Jackson.
Wallbaum added, "Our family appreciates the outpouring of love and support we have received. We hope that love and support extends to those that also serve and protect their communities because Joe considered you to be the extension of our family."
